summary: Presents a few observations on NCP statistics, with measured distributions of NCP message types and IMP message types.

plainLanguage.summary: Someone counted what kinds of messages the network's software sends and reports what turned up.

subtitle: Operating statistics and message patterns from a live ARPANET site

tldr.problem: Early ARPANET operators needed to understand how the network was actually performing and what patterns of traffic emerged.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 618 presents actual statistics collected from the NCP (Network Control Program) at Harvard, including message type counts, error rates, and data message sizes over a one-week period.
tldr.outcome: The data revealed insights about retransmission behavior, allocation strategies across hosts, and that many control messages were not actually separate packets but were combined with data messages.

today: RFC 618 is a historical snapshot of ARPANET operations in early 1974, valuable for understanding how the early network performed and how operators monitored it.

sections.title: NCP Statistics Measurement
sections.content:
RFC 618 presents NCP statistics from the Harvard-10 network interface. The NCP collected counts of different message types, error conditions, and data transfer patterns. After 168 hours of continuous operation (one week), these statistics revealed how the ARPANET actually behaved in practice.

The statistics included counts of control messages like RTS (Request to Send), STR (Send to Receiver), ALL (Allocate), and others, as well as IMP (Interface Message Processor) messages and error conditions.
sections.plainLanguage: The NCP is the software that connects a computer to the network. It kept count of every message it sent and received.

sections.title: Key Observations
sections.content: The RFC highlights three important findings. First, the number of discarded RFNMs (Request for Next Message) equaled the number of timed-out RFNMs, suggesting that messages were delayed rather than lost, pointing to a need for longer timeouts. Second, allocation strategies varied across hosts, with some sending an allocate for every message received while Harvard's strategy of maintaining a desired allocation level reduced overhead. Third, NOP (No Operation) messages were remarkably frequent (about 25% of control messages), though many were combined with other messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages weren't actually disappearing; they were just slow. Different computers used different strategies for managing flow. And the network sent a surprising number of 'do nothing' messages.

sections.title: Data Distribution
sections.content: The statistics included a histogram of received data message sizes, showing that most messages were small (under 128 bits), with significant numbers in larger sizes. The NCP had 72 free buffers with 7% average utilization, indicating network use was moderate at that time.
sections.plainLanguage: The data showed what sizes of messages were most common. Most were small, like a quick note, rather than big files.
